Yaanam Auto Exchange: What Does the Household Hire Instead?

Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu — Sunday, 22 November 2026

1. The night before

The last flight to Chennai had gone and Kavitha Nambiar had let it go. She would take the 6:10 and be at the Guindy office two hours before the board decided where Yaanam Auto Exchange's last ₹72 crore of growth capital would go. Three documents lay on her dining table and would not sit together: her co-founder's pre-read, which said in line two that Yaanam had a Yashodeep problem; a survey closed on 6 November in Singapore, which said eighteen of every hundred lost buyers had gone to an organised used-car retailer at all; and her own options memo, rewritten five times and still not believed.

The discomfort was not thin evidence: there was a great deal of it, pointing four ways, each with a champion whose bonus depended on it. Yaanam had retailed 18,400 cars in the year to 31 March 2026: ₹993.60 crore of revenue at ₹5.40 lakh average price, gross profit ₹77.28 crore. In the half to 30 September it retailed 10,800 against a plan of 12,600 — short by 1,800 units, or 14.3 per cent. Nobody disputed the shortfall, only what it was short against.

2. How Yaanam got here

Kavitha and Balaji Krishnamoorthy started Yaanam in June 2018 in a single yard on Avinashi Road, on the observation that Coimbatore's textile and pump-set economy traded cars constantly and trusted nobody doing it. The first model was consignment: the car stayed with the owner, Yaanam brought buyers and took four per cent. It grew and never earned.

Two decisions still bind the company. In September 2021 Yaanam needed floor-plan funding to stop losing deals to dealers who could pay sellers on the spot. Yashasvi Vehicle Finance, a Chennai NBFC, offered a ₹110 crore inventory line and a lending tie-up in exchange for exclusivity on retail financing at Yaanam's hubs through 31 March 2028. Financing then looked like plumbing, a rail no customer chose a retailer for. Kavitha signed. No second lender can stand at Yaanam's counters without a negotiated release, and the line is recallable on ninety days' notice.

The second came in February 2023, when Yaanam began buying inventory outright and launched Yaanam Assured: a 140-point inspection, a six-month warranty from Yogkshema Assurance Services, a seven-day return. Certification, the founders told investors, was the moat. Yaduvansh Growth Capital led the ₹210 crore Series B of November 2024 and wrote in a covenant: gross profit per retailed unit not below ₹35,000 in any two consecutive quarters. By September 2026 Yaanam ran fourteen hubs in Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka, with engineering in Pune, analytics in Singapore, design in Berlin and remarketing in Dubai.

3. The industry

India sells roughly one-and-a-half used cars for every new one, and almost all of that trade is unorganised: a neighbourhood broker, a garage owner who also flips cars, a cousin who knows a man in Tiruppur. The organised share is what every investor deck measures, and every organised player measures itself against the others — Maruti Suzuki True Value, Mahindra First Choice Wheels, Hyundai Promise, Cars24, Spinny, CarDekho, OLX. Yaanam's dashboards were built on that map, as were the panels of Yugantar Motor Classifieds, bought for ₹18 lakh a year.

Three forces sat outside that map and pressed on the business anyway. New-car prices had risen steeply through the BS-VI and OBD-2 transitions, pushing first-time buyers into used stock but also pushing households to keep an existing car a fourth or fifth year. The Reserve Bank's tightening of risk weights on thin-file consumer credit had made every vehicle-finance NBFC, Yashasvi included, more selective about exactly the customer Yaanam's tier-two hubs attracted. And electric two-wheelers, cab subscriptions and the economics of Uber, Ola and Rapido made it rational for a household in Erode to decide it needed no second car. Add the GST margin scheme, differing state transfer timelines, and the DPDP Act's consent rules, which the legal desk called awkward for the very survey Kavitha wanted to quote. Yaanam's only foreign exposure was Harshad Vora's Dubai desk, moving aged stock to Yamama Motors Trading LLC in Sharjah against a UAE concession expiring 31 March 2027.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Figure 1 — Eight years, and the beliefs that did not survive
Yaanam board minutes; beliefs in brown as recorded at each decision.

In April 2026 Yashodeep Auto Malls, a Hyderabad chain with eleven multi-brand yards, opened in Coimbatore and Kochi: no certification fee, a twelve-month warranty against Yaanam's six, and prices Yaanam's team read as ₹22,000 to ₹30,000 below its own. Walk-ins were quoting Yashodeep by the second week. In June, Yashasvi began declining loans it would have written in March. Nobody connected the two until October: hubs logged declines as finance failures, marketing logged softness as competitive pressure, and the records sat in different systems.

By 30 September the half was 1,800 units light. Then came Deepavali, and October retailed 2,460 units against 2,050 in October 2025, twenty per cent higher — a figure Balaji put on page two of his pre-read. Kavitha asked Nirupama Das in Singapore for something never commissioned before: not a churn model but a destination study. Of the 61,200 who test-drove in the half and took no delivery within ninety days, her team reached 6,000, or 9.8 per cent, and asked one question first — what are you driving now? Those answers are Exhibit 2, and they did not resemble Exhibit 3, which the company had collected all along.

5. The people

Kavitha Nambiar — Co-founder and Chief Product Officer, Coimbatore
Owns the recommendation. Argues the company has measured a market defined by its own category, not by the job customers were doing. Has not told Balaji that two of her four options are one.
Balaji Krishnamoorthy — Co-founder and Chief Executive, Chennai
Wants to match Yashodeep on price and warranty, and to be seen doing it. Incentive: a Series C step-up on a story of category leadership. Is not saying a term sheet is soft-circled, priced off the Yugantar panel.
Farida Kazi — Head of Retail Operations, Coimbatore
Runs all fourteen hubs; believes proximity to the seller is the only variable that ever moved the business, and wants eight more. Is not saying Thrissur and Salem run at two-thirds of underwritten volume, or that she rotates aged stock to flatter days-in-stock.
Nirupama Das — Director of Analytics, Singapore
Built the destination study. Argues fewer than one in five lost buyers went to a competitor the board can name, and the largest destination is a household keeping its own car. Is not volunteering that respondents skew metro, or that legal has flagged the calls.
Anushree Pai — Design Director, Berlin
Six unapproved weeks prototyping a flow in which Yaanam takes over a household's car — service, insurance, buy-back at twenty-four months — before selling it another. Is not saying it has no unit economics, or that it cost four Pune weeks.
Shweta Kulkarni — Head of Credit Partnerships, Pune
Argues the shortfall is an approval-rate story and nothing else, and ₹22 crore of first-loss deposit buys back eleven of the thirteen points lost since April, taking approvals to 68 per cent. Is not saying that 68 still sits two points below April's 70, that Yashasvi called the tightening permanent in July, or that the guarantee cap may not allow it.
Harshad Vora — Head of Remarketing and Exports, Dubai
Wants to clear 600 aged units to Yamama and opposes any cut that reprices the book; measured on units moved, not margin. Is not saying the bid is below carrying cost, or that its duty concession lapses in March.
Ramesh Trivedi — Partner, Yaduvansh Growth Capital, Mumbai
Holds the ₹35,000 covenant and a consent right over deployments above ₹25 crore. Wants an answer legible to the Series C market, meaning one about Yashodeep. Is not saying his fund's own thesis treats organised used-car retail as a low-margin channel.

7. Voices

“Eighteen per cent in the survey, eighteen in the CRM. Two systems, one answer. We are losing to Yashodeep, and I will not be the man who explained it away.”Balaji Krishnamoorthy, strategy call, 10 November 2026
“The two eighteens are not the same eighteen. One names a destination. The other is a dropdown filled in on the way to lunch. Bet ₹72 crore on the second if you like, but call it a choice.”Nirupama Das, same call, 5:40 a.m. in Singapore
“Same Wagon R. My husband said we will manage two more years, the school van is anyway coming. We liked your car. It was not about your car.”Verbatim, respondent 2,114, Tiruppur, destination study
“Nobody in Dharapuram is comparing three websites. They walk into whoever is on the main road. Give me eight hubs and I will give you the units. That survey is a Singapore document.”Farida Kazi, message thread, 16 November 2026
“We spent four years making it easier to compare our cars with other people's cars, and the largest group walking out are not comparing cars. They are deciding whether to spend at all.”Anushree Pai, design review, Berlin, 17 November 2026

8. The options as Kavitha currently sees them

A. Match Yashodeep on price and warranty

Cut ₹18,000 a unit, extend the warranty to twelve months, spend ₹14 crore saying so. Legible to the board, the Series C market and every walk-in quoting a Yashodeep price. Costs ₹33.32 crore in the half and takes margin to ₹24,000, breaching the covenant held by the man who most wants the move.

B. Build the household mobility offer

₹26 crore into Anushree's flow: take over the car's service and insurance, guarantee a buy-back at twenty-four months, sell the replacement then. Aimed at the 25 per cent who kept their car and, arguably, the 5 per cent who subscribed and 7 per cent who took cabs. Unproven, slow, modelled at 1,320 units because the model counts units.

C. Rebuild the finance rail

₹22 crore of first-loss deposit, a second lender at the counters, an own-book pilot. The most direct response to the only monotonic trend. Needs release from the 2021 exclusivity, sits against the guarantee cap, rests on a recovery Yashasvi says is not coming.

D. Eight tier-two hubs

₹32 crore to be on the main road in Dharapuram, Kottayam, Hosur and five more towns, aimed at the 22 per cent who bought from an independent dealer. The only option the company's own history supports — and the most capital, the slowest ramp, the one whose sponsor hides two weak hubs.

Kavitha's difficulty is that these are not four answers to one question. A and D answer “how do we sell more used cars than the other used-car sellers”. C answers “how do we let the customers we convinced actually pay”. B answers a question nobody at Yaanam has written down.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

  • Money. ₹72 crore uncommitted; the four options total ₹94 crore. Anything above ₹25 crore needs Yaduvansh's consent.
  • Covenant. Gross profit per retailed unit not below ₹35,000 in any two consecutive quarters; Q2 FY27 was ₹42,000.
  • Contract. Yashasvi's exclusivity runs to 31 March 2028; its ₹110 crore inventory line, against a ₹244.44 crore book, is recallable on ninety days' notice; the renewal window opens 31 December 2026.
  • Regulation. The guarantee cap limits Option C's structure; the DPDP consent question hangs over the research calls that produced Exhibit 2.
  • People. Hiring freeze until Q4 FY27; four Pune engineering weeks already spent on an unapproved prototype.
  • Windows. The Yamama bid lapses 30 November; the UAE concession 31 March 2027; the board meets at 11 a.m. on 23 November.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. List, from Exhibits 2 and 3, everything Yaanam's customers hired instead. Which appear in the competitive dashboard, and which do not?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 agree on 18 per cent. What would you need to know before treating that agreement as corroboration?
  3. Exhibit 4 is the best-looking document in the pack, and priced a term sheet. What does its denominator exclude, and how does that change what a reader concludes?
  4. Exhibit 5 shows the only trend moving in one direction. Is it the cause of the shortfall, a symptom of the same change, or a constraint every option must survive?
  5. Exhibit 7 gives every option a figure for incremental units. What does that unit undervalue, and how would you rebuild the comparison so Options A and B can be judged honestly?
  6. It is Monday morning, 23 November. Kavitha has forty minutes and one recommendation. What does she recommend, what does she do with the ₹72 crore, what does she say to Ramesh Trivedi about the covenant — and what would she tell the board Yaanam competes against?

11. Sunday, late

At a quarter past eleven Kavitha printed Exhibits 2 and 4 and set them side by side under the lamp. Both were true. One was about her company, the other about her customers, and she could not say which the forty minutes belonged to. Her phone showed a message from Harshad asking whether he could tell Yamama yes before the bid lapsed, and an unsent draft to Ramesh, subject line covenant — a question. She turned off the lamp at midnight with both pages lying there, and the flight was at ten past six.
exp20v2-comp.jobs.competition:
Strategy & Business · Competitive Strategy & Moats

Competing on the job, not the category

Your real competitor is whatever the customer hires today — including doing nothing at all.

1. The slide Meera didn't want to give

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Meera Iyer stood before Labh Money's board in Bengaluru with a slide she had rewritten four times and still did not believe. Labh Money was a three-year-old expense-tracking and micro-savings app for gig workers, delivery riders and small kirana traders — Indians paid in cash or irregular UPI credits, not a fixed salary. The Series B, closed eight months earlier at ₹86 crore, had been underwritten on reaching 40 lakh monthly active users by March 2027. The company had 9.2 lakh.

The obvious explanation, chased for eighteen months, was Gathri Finance — a better-funded rival, ₹210 crore raised, with a near-identical UPI-linked auto-save engine, bill-splitting and expense-diary screen. Every month Meera's team opened its release notes and matched whatever had shipped. By September, feature parity was essentially complete. Week-eight retention still stalled at nineteen percent, on both apps. Matching Gathri Finance feature for feature had not moved the number that mattered, and Meera was about to tell her board the fix was more of the thing that had not worked.

What changed the slide was a data packet her research lead, Priya Ramesh, dropped on her desk three weeks earlier: forty interviews, then a 1,240-person survey run with Naveen Pillai's data team in Gurugram, asking one question — not "which app do you use," but "the last time you needed to know how much you could safely spend before payday, what did you actually do?" Gathri Finance barely appeared. The category — other budgeting apps — was rarely what Labh Money was actually up against.

Fig. 1 — The category map puts Labh Money inside a small ring of look-alike apps. The job map asks what the customer actually hired last time the job arose, and puts five non-category options ahead of both apps.

2. The idea

Job-based competition defines your competitive set by the task the customer is trying to get done, not the shelf your product sits on. A category competitor sells a similar product through a similar channel; a job competitor is anything — a product, a habit, a person, or doing nothing — the customer currently "hires" to make progress on a specific struggle. The two sets overlap far less than most roadmaps assume.

The idea solves a specific blind spot in ordinary competitive analysis: a category list, drawn from app-store rankings or funding databases, only contains firms that already decided to build the same kind of product you did. It says nothing about the larger set of people solving the same underlying problem with a spreadsheet, a phone call, a neighbour, or a shrug. Theodore Levitt named the underlying error in 1960 — "people don't want a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole" — and Clayton Christensen, with the consultant Bob Moesta, turned it into a practical method through the 2000s, most famously in a study of why a fast-food chain's milkshakes sold best before 8 a.m.: commuters weren't comparing milkshakes to other milkshakes, but to bananas, bagels and boredom on a long drive. The sentence Meera could repeat without sounding glib is this: find out what the customer is really hiring you to do, and your competitive set is everything else hired for that job, including doing nothing.

3. How it actually works

The method has four steps, and the one practitioners skip is the first: naming the job precisely enough to exclude things. "Help me manage my money" is not a job statement; it fits every fintech product and rules nothing out. "Know, on the Thursday before payday, whether I can afford the LPG cylinder without asking my brother-in-law again" is one — a trigger moment, a felt anxiety, a social dimension. A usable job has a functional dimension (the arithmetic), an emotional one (the anxiety of guessing wrong) and, often in Indian household and small-trader contexts, a social one — who you would have to ask, and what that costs.

Second, list everything currently hired for that exact job — not "money apps," but the full, unglamorous set: WhatsApp family groups posting running totals, the neighbourhood chit fund or committee (bishi, kitty), a paper diary beside the till, an informal tab with the kirana shopkeeper, asking a spouse, or keeping a number in one's head. This is where category-trained teams get uncomfortable, because none of these "competitors" show up in a funding database or a Play Store search.

Third, map the switch moment — the event that makes someone fire their current method. Bob Moesta's later "four forces" work names the tension well: a push (something about the old way that now hurts, like a missed EMI) and a pull (an attractive new option) must outweigh the anxiety of the new and the habit-gravity of the old, or nothing moves, however good the feature list. Fourth, size the job, not the category — count everyone with the underlying struggle, not just those already buying something like yours; the gap between those numbers is usually the whole opportunity.

4. The worked example

Priya's 1,240-person survey, run across gig and informal-trade workers in Bengaluru, Pune and Lucknow, asked what people had actually hired last time the "safe-to-spend-before-payday" job arose. The old, category-based sizing started from India's roughly 3.2 crore dedicated-budgeting-app users — Gathri Finance and its peers — and, conservatively, assumed a realistic addressable pool of 1.6 crore.

What was hired last timeShare of surveyApprox. respondents
WhatsApp family/friend expense group34%421

Fig. 2 — Category rivals accounted for one respondent in twenty. Five other "competitors," none of them an app, accounted for the rest.

Reframed by job, the addressable population is not the 3.2 crore who already use a budgeting app but everyone with the underlying struggle: India's irregular-income workforce — gig, daily-wage and small-trade earners — runs to roughly 15 crore. If a dedicated app serves only 5% of that (about 75 lakh), the job-based market is nearly ten times the category-based one on paper. But a market on paper is not a plan; the second pass narrows the population to those most likely to actually switch. Restricting the job to urban, digitally-paid gig workers, for whom a digital tool is a small behavioural step, shrinks the base to about 6.4 crore. Of those, roughly 30% had hit a concrete push trigger in the last three months (a missed EMI, a bounced auto-pay, a fight over a shopkeeper's tab): 6.4 crore × 30% = 1.92 crore "triggered" job-holders. Assuming 12% of that triggered population converts over eighteen months — a rate from Priya's interviews, not Meera's old plan — gives 1.92 crore × 12% ≈ 23 lakh projected activations, against roughly 8 lakh under the category-based plan (1.6 crore × an assumed 5% conversion). Narrowing the population shrank the number before it grew it, and arithmetic, not ambition, made the board slide credible.

5. The nuances a learner must hold onto

It does not replace category discipline, it precedes it

Being the best-hired solution to a job still requires adequacy on category dimensions — reliability, price, UPI integration. Job-based thinking explains why you are hired or fired; it does not excuse a product that does not work.

It is not a customer-needs survey

"Needs" statements ("I need to manage my money better") are abstract and timeless; job statements are concrete and dated. Teams that skip the moment produce persona slides that read well and predict nothing.

It works best where switching is discrete and describable

Where purchases are driven by impulse or status — a sneaker, a wedding outfit — the functional job explains less than what owning the thing signals to others; mapping still applies but needs a social-signalling lens on top.

It cannot tell you willingness to pay

A larger job map is not a larger revenue line. Meera's 23-lakh figure is an activation estimate, not a monetisation one; converting job-holders into payers needs its own test.

Non-consumption is usually the biggest, least visible rival

The 10% "mental math only" and much of the 22% "paper diary" segment were not choosing a solution so much as tolerating one; they are often the largest addressable group precisely because no one else serves them.

The map can be stretched until it means nothing

Pushed far enough, almost anything competes with almost anything — a savings app "competes with sleep." Bounding the job to a specific trigger, as in section three, keeps the exercise usable rather than merely clever.

6. Where the picture changes

In consumer products like Labh Money, the job is often part functional and part social — the WhatsApp group wins not because its arithmetic is better but because it is visible to family, supplying accountability a diary cannot. In B2B, the job map needs drawing per role: a finance controller's job (an audit trail surviving a GST reconciliation) is not a sales rep's job (a claim reimbursed by the weekend), and one "customer job" often hides two buyers switching for two reasons. In a marketplace, the map runs twice, once per side: a rider's job might be "make my daily income predictable," rivalled by one steady restaurant contract, not another platform; a merchant's job might be "get today's cash flow right," rivalled by a distributor's informal credit line. Early-stage firms gain most from this lens, having no category position to defend; incumbents drift back toward category benchmarking by habit, since competitive-intelligence teams and filings with bodies like SEBI or the RBI are organised by category, quietly pulling strategy back even after a job-based insight has been proven.

7. Common mistakes

Matching the competitor's changelog. Symptom: a roadmap mirroring a rival's release notes, as Labh Money's did for eighteen months. Error: treating the category rival as the only real alternative. Diagnostic: ask ten retained users what they used the week before they tried you; if "nothing" or a non-category answer dominates, the roadmap is set by the wrong list.

Writing the job too broadly. Symptom: a job statement vague enough that any feature is justified by it. Error: skipping the trigger moment. Diagnostic: if the statement fits on a mission poster, it is not a job statement yet — it needs a day, a feeling and a specific decision attached.

Writing off non-consumers as "not a market." Symptom: treating anyone not already paying a competitor as low-priority. Error: forgetting a large population enduring a high-effort workaround is the classic entry point for a new product. Diagnostic: measure the effort and anxiety of the workaround, not just its price — a free but painful alternative is often more vulnerable than a well-funded one.

Freezing the map after one round. Symptom: a job map from a research sprint eighteen months ago still guiding decisions. Error: treating the competitive set as fixed as adjacent categories add features that absorb the job — a UPI app adding a budgeting nudge, say. Diagnostic: re-run the "what did you fire" question every couple of quarters, not once a year.

8. What good looks like

Six months later, Labh Money's roadmap was organised by job-holder segment and fired incumbent, not feature parity with Gathri Finance. It shipped a shareable weekly spending summary meant for forwarding into the same WhatsApp groups it had been losing to, turning a rival into a distribution channel, and an "advance against next payout" nudge timed to the anxiety before rent or an LPG refill was due — aimed at the shopkeeper's tab and the informal chit, not Gathri Finance. Week-eight retention rose from nineteen to thirty-four percent over two quarters, driven almost entirely by users who had never used a competing app — the non-consumption segment the category map had never shown Meera.

9. What Meera decided, and what to sit with

Meera's board slide kept one comparison to Gathri Finance — a short table showing parity on table-stakes features — and spent the rest on the job map, the non-consumption arithmetic, and the two features aimed at WhatsApp groups and the payday-tab moment. The reasoning was not that Gathri Finance no longer mattered, but that it had stopped being where the next million users come from. Next, she asked Naveen and Priya to study Bob Moesta's fuller four-forces model, to design around anxiety and habit deliberately, and later the opposite move — deliberate category design — for the point Labh Money would need to name a new category rather than serve old jobs better than anyone else.

Two questions worth sitting with: if you listed everything your users fired in the last ninety days, would your acknowledged competitors even appear? And is your product's ceiling set by a rival's feature set, or by the "doing nothing" segment you have not yet made anxious enough to switch?
exp40v2-comp.jobs.competition:
Strategy & Business · Competitive Strategy & Moats · Exp40

Competing on the job, not the category

What does the customer hire today instead of us? The answer is rarely on the competitor slide.

1. Two rooms, ten days apart

On 14 July 2026, in a converted mill office off Ashram Road in Ahmedabad, Rukmini Deshpande opened the weekly pipeline review at Chhaanv Rooftop Energy with a number she had been avoiding. Chhaanv, founded in 2021, installed 3–5 kW residential rooftop solar across Gujarat, with an app that showed households their generation and savings. It had raised ₹48 crore in November 2025 against a plan to reach 12,000 cumulative installations by March 2028. In July 2026 it had 2,150. Acquisition cost had risen from ₹6,800 to ₹9,400 per installation over five quarters while Chhaanv's quoted price per watt fell nine percent. The company tracked eleven other empanelled installers in the state on a shared sheet — price per watt, inverter brand, warranty years, app features — and won on most of those columns. Harish Nambiar, the CFO, in Chennai, put it plainly: the plan needed either three times the leads at the same cost, or a different definition of the market.

Ten days later and 1,300 kilometres south, Aparna Sundaram sat in Coimbatore with the FY26 loss report of Kasauti Quality Systems, which sold camera-based defect inspection for auto-component lines at ₹42 lakh a year per plant, fourteen plants live, mostly tier-one suppliers to passenger-vehicle OEMs. Of 41 qualified opportunities, 61 percent ended in no decision and 11 percent went to a named software rival. The CRM loss-reason field said "budget." The transcripts were more specific: in at least nine plants the quality head had answered the trigger Kasauti sold against — an OEM complaint — by hiring two inspectors at roughly ₹2.4 lakh a year each.

Both companies had a competitor list, and both were wrong in the same way: each contained only firms that had already decided to build the same kind of thing.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Job-based competition defines the competitive set by the progress a customer is trying to make in a specific situation, not by the seller's category. A job is a struggle, arising at an identifiable moment, that a customer resolves by hiring something; a competitor is anything hired for it — a product from another category, a person, a habit, a policy parameter, or the decision to tolerate the struggle. The category set is only the subset sharing your form factor and channel.

The problem it solves is a measurement artefact. Category lists are drawn from where supply is registered — app stores, funding databases, GST codes — so they exclude everyone who resolves the same struggle without buying anything classified as your product. Theodore Levitt's 1960 "Marketing Myopia" named the error; Christensen and Moesta made it operational through the 2000s with switch interviews, the milkshake study, and the claim that non-consumption is the largest untapped market. The proposition is narrow and strong: your real competitor is whatever the customer hires today, and it is usually not in your category.

Four schools would not sign that sentence in the same form. Anthony Ulwick's outcome-driven branch signs "the job is stable and measurable" — decomposable into dozens of desired-outcome statements rated for importance and satisfaction — but not that it must be discovered narratively. Moesta's branch signs the reverse: the unit of analysis is the moment of switch, with its push, pull, anxiety and habit, and outcome lists mistake tidiness for truth. The positioning and category-design school, descended from Ries and Trout, signs "buyers shop a mental category before a brand; a product without a category the buyer recognises is invisible," and will not draw the competitor set from jobs rather than from the shelf the buyer stands in front of. The industrial-organisation school in Porter's line signs "profitability is set by the structure of a defined industry" and cannot admit habits, since rivalry, concentration and entry barriers are not computable against one — the objection the Competition Commission of India faces when it defines a relevant market by demand substitutability. The Ehrenberg-Bass school around Byron Sharp signs "growth comes from mental and physical availability across category entry points, not need-segmentation," in direct conflict with the non-consumption claim. Section 10 returns to these rather than dissolving them.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice has four steps, of which the first and last are usually skipped. Step one writes the job with a date, a feeling and an exclusion. "Help households save on electricity" is not a job statement; it justifies any feature. Sheetal Barot, running Chhaanv's field research from Rajkot, wrote instead: "It is the second week of May, my bill has crossed ₹4,000 twice, the inverter battery died in last week's outage, and I must decide what to spend ₹20,000 on." That sentence excludes things, which is its purpose.

Step two enumerates what was actually hired at that moment. Chhaanv surveyed 900 owner-occupier households across Ahmedabad, Rajkot, Surat and Vadodara, asking not which solar brand they preferred but what they last did when the bill or the supply became a problem.

What the household hired last time the job aroseShareRespondents
Bought or replaced an inverter-battery unit31%279
Replaced appliances (5-star AC, BLDC fans, LEDs)24%216
Rationed use — cut AC hours, switched off the geyser19%171
Approached the discom on tariff, load or a disputed bill9%81
Nothing — absorbed the bill12%108
Rooftop solar, any installer5%45

Exhibit 1 — Chhaanv's survey, n = 900, June 2026. A battery cost about ₹22,000, an installation ₹1.85 lakh. Of the 45 households that went solar, 13 chose Chhaanv: a 29 percent category share, a 1.4 percent share of hires for the job.

That pair — 29 percent of the category, 1.4 percent of the job — is the argument in miniature, and the first quantity an expert computes. Call it hire share: your hires over all hires for the job, not all hires in your category. A firm can hold a commanding category share while being a rounding error on the job, and every internal incentive reports the first number.

Step three sizes the job through its trigger rather than its population. Naive job sizing produces an absurdity — every household has an electricity bill — so the disciplined version narrows before it widens. Gujarat has roughly 31 lakh urban owner-occupied households with a shade-free roof and a connected load of 2 kW or more; about 44 percent own an inverter-battery unit, or 13.6 lakh. Batteries last around four years, so some 3.4 lakh households a year face a ₹18,000–₹26,000 replacement, and 38 percent of those had a summer bill above ₹3,000 a month: 1.29 lakh triggered households a year. A Rajkot pilot converted 9 percent reached at that moment — about 11,600 installations a year from one trigger, against a category plan of 1.1 lakh annual state installations × 8 percent target share = 8,800. The size is not the point.

Step four, almost always left implicit, re-derives unit economics through the new channel, because a different competitor implies a different place to stand: reaching a household the week its battery dies means standing in an inverter dealer's shop, not bidding on search terms against eleven installers.

Exhibit 2 — The job map's payoff at Chhaanv was not a bigger market but a cheaper seam into it. Identical product, identical gross margin; the competitor you name determines the channel you buy, and the channel sets CAC.

The second-order effect matters more than the headline. Once Chhaanv accepted that its rival was a ₹22,000 battery rather than a ₹1.9 lakh competing installation, the comparison changed from "which solar company" to "solar versus battery," and the product had to answer it: a financed offer at ₹2,450 a month against ₹22,000 in cash every four years, plus a backup-during-outage claim, since what the battery did and the panels did not was keep a fan running at 2 a.m. The central rooftop subsidy and Gujarat's net-metering regime stopped being marketing headlines and became the instruments that put the monthly figure below the battery's amortised cost. None of that follows from a category comparison.

4. When it applies, stated as tests

Three testable conditions separate the cases where the lens pays from those where it misleads. Does the job have a datable trigger? Chhaanv passes — a dead battery and a May bill are dated events; so does Kasauti, since an OEM complaint is documented and dated. Is the total cost of the current hire observable? Chhaanv passes; ₹22,000 every four years is a price anyone can quote. Kasauti fails partially, because the incumbent's cost is an expected value over an event whose probability nobody in the plant will state aloud. Is the switch a discrete decision by one identifiable person? Chhaanv passes; Kasauti fails, since plant head, quality head and corporate finance each carry a different job, and treating them as one customer produced a value story that persuaded none of them.

The lens actively misleads in three situations: habitual repeat purchases, where there is no switch moment to interview and availability predicts behaviour better; status purchases, where the functional job is a small part of the decision; and mandated purchases — a statutory audit, a prescribed disclosure — where the job is compliance, the set collapses to the approved-vendor list, and category analysis is simply correct.

5. Hard edge cases, and the organisational seams

The competitor that is a policy parameter

Khasra Title Intelligence, an AI-native firm in Jaipur, sells automated title-and-encumbrance analysis over digitised land records at ₹900 a report, against a panel advocate's ₹4,500 opinion. It kept losing deals it had apparently won on price and speed. The reason, surfaced in a credit-committee meeting, was that lenders had a cheaper hire for the job "be confident enough to lend against this plot": they cut loan-to-value from 70 percent to 55 and priced the uncertainty instead of resolving it. That hire costs nothing on any line item — it appears as ₹6 lakh of foregone loan on a ₹40 lakh property, borne by a customer absent from the vendor comparison. A competitor made of a number in a credit policy is invisible to every category tool, and beating it means quantifying the foregone book and selling to the business head, not operations.

Two-sided markets need two maps, and the seam between them is organisational

Chunri Fabric Exchange, a Surat B2B marketplace for woven fabric, ran a supply team benchmarking against other exchanges and a demand team benchmarking against brokers. Both were right about their own side, which is why the roadmap fight was unresolvable. A weaver's job is "keep the looms loaded next week," whose incumbent is a job-work order from a larger trader, not a platform. A buyer's job is "land 4,000 metres of a matched lot before the festive season," whose incumbent is his broker of eighteen years. That second map humbled the pricing team: on an ₹18 lakh order the broker's two percent is ₹36,000, but 45 days of credit is worth ₹39,945 at an 18 percent cost of funds, so the broker is net free — while Chunri's 1.2 percent with seven-day payment is a real ₹21,600 cost. A lower take rate lost to a higher one, because the hire being compared included working capital the exchange had left out of its own product.

Regulated products: the job map changes the packaging, not the pitch

Chhatri Livestock Insurance, an IRDAI-regulated micro-insurance venture in Indore, sold ₹65,000 of cover on a milch animal for ₹2,600 a year. Its category rivals were other cattle policies; its job rival was a distress sale, which recovers about ₹36,000 of a ₹65,000 animal, leaving a ₹29,000 loss at roughly 3.5 percent annual mortality — an expected loss of ₹1,015 against a ₹2,600 premium. The farmer's incumbent hire was rational, and no education beats that on expected value. What sold was a change of form: collected through the dairy co-operative's daily milk payment as a ₹9 deduction across 289 collection days, the identical premium converted at 19 percent instead of 4. The job was never "insure my buffalo" but "never have to ask a relative for money in a bad week," and the lump sum, not the price, was the obstacle. Regulated categories constrain what may be bundled and how it is described, so the seam here is product and compliance.

AI-native products face a hire that improves without them

Khasra's second problem is general to AI-native firms: the first thing a customer hires for a reasoning job is a general assistant they already pay for, and it improves every quarter without Khasra shipping anything. If Khasra's accuracy becomes routine, the job is absorbed into the lender's origination system and the competitor becomes whichever workflow vendor bundles it. Mature companies handle this less elegantly than they describe: a category-benchmarked roadmap for salespeople who need a comparison grid to survive procurement, and a separate job-based programme for two or three bets — workable only while someone senior arbitrates which list wins.

6. Five distinctions that separate the expert

The map often reveals a price ceiling, not a bigger market

Kasauti's map did not expand its opportunity; it explained its losses. Against the job "make sure an OEM complaint never reaches the managing director's desk," the incumbent hire was two inspectors at ₹4.8 lakh a year plus a tolerated risk: a ₹31 lakh line-stoppage penalty at about 35 percent annual probability, an expected ₹10.85 lakh. Total incumbent cost ₹15.65 lakh against a ₹42 lakh licence. The tell is a high no-decision rate with almost no losses to named rivals. The obvious reading — no budget — is wrong: the buyer has an alternative cheaper in expectation, and the product is priced above what the job is worth. Kasauti could reprice or find larger stakes, and did both.

"Nothing" is almost never nothing

The 12 percent of Chhaanv's households that "absorbed the bill" and the 19 percent who rationed were not passive; they paid in discomfort, in argument, in a July evening without a fan. The tell is a survey category labelled with an absence. Measure the effort and anxiety of the workaround, not its price: a free-but-painful incumbent is often more vulnerable than a funded rival — but only when the pain has a moment attached. Chronic discomfort produces no switch.

Hire share, not category share, is the operating metric

Chhaanv's 29 percent category share went to the board monthly; its 1.4 percent hire share had never been computed. Every internal system — competitive intelligence, pricing benchmarks, analyst notes — is organised by category, so category share regenerates itself. The tell is a share figure whose denominator nobody can name in customer terms.

What usually changes is the channel, not the feature

Teams expect a job map to yield a feature. More often it yields a place to stand and a form to sell in: a dealer's counter, a ₹9 deduction at a milk centre. The tell is a team that ran switch interviews and emerged with a backlog item rather than a distribution change. Features answer the pull; channel and packaging answer anxiety and habit — and those two usually keep the incumbent hired.

Job maps expire, and they expire from the side

A map is accurate only as of its trigger. When an adjacent product absorbs that trigger — a battery brand adding a solar-ready hybrid inverter, a loan-origination vendor bundling title checks — the incumbent set changes with no new entrant in your category. The tell is a map over four quarters old quoted as fact. The mirror-image risk is stretch: once a team learns its competitor is not another app, every adjacent struggle looks like the same job, and the map loses its power to exclude. There the tell is a job statement that has lost its date, and section 8 has the case.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the job is part functional and part social, and the incumbent often wins on visibility rather than performance: Chhaanv's real obstacle in several households was a father-in-law who had bought the battery. In B2B the job must be drawn per role, and one deal often contains three jobs with three incumbents. In marketplaces the map runs once per side and the difficulty is organisational, as at Chunri. In hardware the incumbent hire is frequently the installed base itself and switching costs are physical, which makes trigger timing decisive rather than merely helpful. In AI products the distinctive features are a competitor that improves autonomously and the risk of the job being absorbed upward into a workflow. Across stages the difference is real at the extremes and overstated in the middle: early-stage firms gain most, having no category position to defend, while large incumbents drift back because reporting, pricing committees and analyst relationships are built on categories. For a mid-stage company the binding constraint is sequencing, not insight: a job-based bet needs a channel rebuilt, and that takes two or three quarters the plan did not budget.

8. Three worked examples, including one failure

Chhaanv. Reframing the incumbent from eleven installers to a ₹22,000 battery moved planned FY27 contribution from ₹25.2 crore to ₹38.1 crore; a year on, installations ran at 890 a month against 410. Chhatri. Identical premium, cover and regulator; conversion from 4 to 19 percent by changing the comparison and the payment form. In both, the map's output was a channel.

Kaarwan Commute Networks — the failure. Kaarwan, a Hyderabad employee-transport operator, began with a good insight: the job was "reach a 7 a.m. shift without losing ninety minutes and my temper," and its incumbent was the employee's own two-wheeler plus the employer's reimbursement policy, not other bus operators. Acting on it took occupancy from 54 to 71 percent of seats in three quarters. Then the map stretched: if the job was really "make the working day bearable," cab pooling, e-bike rentals and hostel beds near industrial parks were all the same job. Burn went from ₹1.1 crore to ₹4.3 crore a month across four businesses; occupancy fell to 48 percent, where cost per seat was ₹4,900 against a ₹3,600 employer price — a ₹1,300 monthly loss per seat. The failure was not the job lens but the lost exclusion clause: a job statement without a trigger cannot say no to anything. Recovery took eleven months. Kaarwan exited three businesses, re-bounded the job to one dated trigger — the employer's obligation under state shops-and-establishments rules to provide transport for women on night shifts — and rebuilt two corridors. Occupancy reached 83 percent, cost per seat fell to ₹2,950, contribution turned positive at ₹650 per seat, and burn settled at ₹1.4 crore: a strategy narrower than the original, not broader.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Mirroring a rival's changelogParity achieved, no metric movementWhat did our last fifty retained customers use the week before they bought?Quarters of undifferentiated engineering
Job written too broadlyStatement fits a wall poster, excludes nothingWhat does this statement forbid us from building?Kaarwan's ₹3.2 crore of extra monthly burn
Pricing above the job's worthHigh no-decision rate, few named-rival lossesWhat does the incumbent hire cost in total, including expected losses?A sales year at 61 percent no-decision
Non-consumers dismissed as "not a market"Segmentation starts from category buyersHow much effort and anxiety does the free alternative impose?Largest segment ceded to a later entrant
One job across several buying rolesChampion keen, deal stalls above themWhose job does the approver have, and what does he hire today?Pipeline that forecasts, never closes

Exhibit 3 — Each diagnostic is answerable from evidence the team already holds; the failure is rarely missing data.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Position one: category salience beats job maps. In its strongest form the Ehrenberg-Bass argument is empirical: brand growth across hundreds of categories tracks penetration and availability, buyers are light and inattentive, and they retrieve brands through category entry points rather than reasoning about struggles. On that evidence Chhaanv's ₹38.1 crore is channel arbitrage in job language, and the durable move is to be the solar brand a Gujarati household can name. It would be wrong if switching in infrequent, high-ticket purchases ran on triggers rather than salience — exactly the class Chhaanv sells, and where that evidence is thinnest.

Position two: jobs are stable and enumerable, not narratively discovered. Ulwick's case rests on the reproducibility of outcome statements: "inspect a machined part for surface defects" has had the same outcomes for decades, and importance-satisfaction gaps find opportunity more reliably than interviews run by people looking for a story. Kasauti's history supports it — the job did not change, only the technology. It would be wrong if the value sits in the competitive set rather than the outcome set, since an outcome list is silent about what the customer hires today.

Position three: non-consumption is not a market. The strongest version is disciplined rather than dismissive: a claim you cannot price, size from observable transactions, or defend before a competition authority is not strategy. Chhatri's arithmetic is the evidence — the self-insuring farmer was rational, and four in five still do not buy. It would be wrong if the barrier for non-consumers were reliably form and friction rather than value, in which case expected value measures the wrong thing; Chhatri's ₹9 deduction is one data point, and one is not a resolution.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs switch interviews and produces a wider competitor slide. Someone who has internalised it computes a denominator before an opportunity, and expects the first output of a map to be uncomfortable — the price is too high, the channel is wrong, the deal has three buyers. They write job statements that forbid things and treat a map as perishable. They can argue the Ehrenberg-Bass position against their own analysis without flinching, and they know which list governs which decision: category discipline for table stakes, pricing and procurement; job analysis for where to stand, what to bundle and whom to sell. Most of all they notice when their organisation has quietly reverted, because it always does.

12. What each protagonist decided

Rukmini Deshpande kept one category comparison slide — parity on price per watt, inverter brand and warranty — and rebuilt the FY27 plan around the battery-replacement trigger: a dealer channel, a ₹2,450-a-month financed offer against ₹22,000 every four years, an outage-backup claim. She accepted a two-quarter dip in installations while the channel was built, and told the board the plan's risk had moved from demand to partner execution.

Aparna Sundaram did the harder thing and cut price: a ₹13.5 lakh single-line tier beneath the ₹15.65 lakh incumbent hire, the ₹42 lakh platform reserved for EV battery-pack traceability where expected loss exceeds ₹1 crore, and a value story per role — cost avoidance for the quality head, audit readiness for the plant head, penalty variance for finance. She stopped reporting share of the inspection-software market, since nobody could name its denominator.

Three questions. If Chhaanv's hire share is 1.4 percent, is its problem competitive, or a distribution problem wearing a competitive costume — and does the distinction change what it should do? Kasauti's map told it to charge less: when is that the right conclusion rather than a failure of nerve? And Chhatri's farmer was rational on expected value yet switched when the form changed — does that vindicate the non-consumption thesis, or show that the barrier was never competition at all?

13. Going deeper

  1. Jobs to Be Done — the parent method: switch interviews and the four forces that supply a map's evidence.
  2. Competitive analysis — widened, not replaced; still needed for table stakes and procurement.
  3. Right to win — what do you have that the other hires for this job do not?
  4. Moats and the 7 Powers — why a job win persists or erodes; advantage versus head start.
  5. Network effects — why marketplace maps like Chunri's compound on one side only.
  6. Switching costs and lock-in — habit-gravity quantified: what firing the incumbent costs.
  7. Moats in the AI era — the Khasra problem: what is defensible when the alternative improves without you.
  8. Positioning — the counterweight, held in tension rather than resolved.
case20v1-comp.jobs.competition:
Gyanodaya Learning: Competing on the Job, Not the Category

Patna, Bihar — 6 October 2026

1. The morning after the sale

It was the Monday after Dussehra, and the Gyanodaya Learning office on Boring Road in Patna still smelled of marigold garlands from the reception shrine. Aparna Sinha, founder and chief executive, had ten days before the board met on 16 October to approve how the company would deploy its next two quarters of growth capital — ₹8 crore, the largest discretionary sum the board had ever handed her at once. The provocation: a screenshot of Gurukul Exam Cloud's Navratri sale, its flagship plan cut from ₹4,200 to ₹3,150, a quarter off, across every exam category Gyanodaya also served. The obvious boardroom read was that Gyanodaya had a Gurukul problem and the ₹8 crore should go toward matching it. A week earlier Aparna had asked her data science lead in Toronto to test that instinct. The analysis had landed the previous evening, and it did not say what the board expected.

2. Company background

Aparna founded Gyanodaya Learning in 2019 after two years preparing for the SSC CGL exam out of a rented room in Muzaffarpur, supplementing an expensive coaching class with photocopied notes passed hand to hand. The product was a bilingual, Hindi-and-English subscription app for competitive government-job exams — SSC CGL and CHSL, IBPS clerk and PO, state police and teaching recruitment — built around mock tests calibrated to each exam board's pattern, recorded lectures, and a doubt-clearing queue of exam-qualified tutors. By March 2026 the company had 1,35,000 paying subscribers and ARR of ₹60.75 crore, on an average price of ₹4,500 a year, reaching aspirants across roughly four hundred towns in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Jharkhand. The recognisable names in exam-prep edtech — Byju's, Unacademy, PhysicsWallah, Testbook — had all pulled back from the aggressive discounting that once defined the sector. Gurukul Exam Cloud, a Bengaluru rival on its third funding round, was the one still spending that way, and its cut was why Aparna's phone had not stopped buzzing since Friday.

3. The situation

The board's concern was not unreasonable on its face. Gurukul's price was now 30 per cent below Gyanodaya's ₹4,500, and renewals had softened: of the 40,000 subscriptions due between April and September 2026, only 18,400 renewed, a rate of 46 per cent, leaving 21,600 lapsed — Exhibit 1. Meera Chandran, head of data science in Toronto, built an exit-survey model rather than assume the cause, reaching 14,000 of the lapsed by in-app prompt and follow-up call. Only 16 per cent named a rival app — mostly Gurukul — as what they turned to instead (Exhibit 2). The rest had gone somewhere the category map missed: forty per cent to an in-person coaching institute, thirty per cent to free WhatsApp, Telegram and YouTube channels, fourteen per cent had stopped preparing. From Singapore, Priya Raghavan, VP customer success, confirmed the pattern from her renewal calls: "my local sir's batch starts next month" came up far more than any mention of Gurukul. From New Jersey, Vikram Oberoi, head of institutional sales, added a complication: Gulmohar Learning Circle, a Dubai coaching network licensing Gyanodaya's content on a ₹40 lakh annual contract, had cited Gurukul's cut in its own renewal talks that week — the institutional side watched the category rivalry even as retail's real losses lay elsewhere.

4. The people

Aparna Sinha — Founder and CEO, Patna
Must bring the board one recommendation for the ₹8 crore budget by 16 October; wary of a decision driven by what is easiest to explain, not what the data supports.
Meera Chandran — Head of Data Science, Toronto
Built the churn and exit-survey analysis behind Exhibits 1 and 2; argues the company has diagnosed its competition by category out of habit, not evidence.
Karan Mehta — Partner, Godavari Growth Partners (board member), Mumbai
Wants a fast, legible response to Gurukul ahead of Series C diligence in November, when investors will ask how Gyanodaya answered the cut.
Vikram Oberoi — Head of Institutional Sales, New Jersey
Manages Gulmohar Learning Circle and similar diaspora-coaching prospects; worried a discount war would cheapen Gyanodaya's standing with institutional buyers who pay for quality.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the number the board already had: renewal had softened to 46 per cent, and Gurukul's cut was the most visible change at the same time. But a softened renewal rate only says subscribers left — not where they went, which is the question this case turns on: a company's real competitor is whatever the customer hires instead, not merely the rival in the same category.

The job an aspirant hires is not "an exam-prep app"; it is "help me pass this exam and feel confident I will" — and for most lapsed subscribers that job was still being filled, just not by anything on Gyanodaya's category map.

Exhibit 3 puts a rupee figure on the diagnosis. Funding all three would cost ₹10.50 crore against an ₹8 crore envelope, and bandwidth allows only one initiative. None turns a profit in year one; the honest comparison is which buys the most durable retention per rupee, aimed at where subscribers actually went.

6. The options

Option A — Match Gurukul's price cut

Cut the annual plan 25 per cent to ₹3,375 and spend ₹3.5 crore promoting it. Upside: a legible answer for the board and Series C diligence, recovering the 3,456 subscribers genuinely price-shopping. Cost: a net first-year loss of ₹4.40 crore, since the discount also applies to subscribers who were never leaving, and 84 per cent of churn goes unaddressed.

Option B — Invest in the hybrid-trust model

Spend ₹4.2 crore on what the coaching institute and the WhatsApp group offer that the app does not: regional mentors in the ten highest-lapse towns, weekly hybrid centres for doubt-clearing, and a WhatsApp-native doubt queue. Upside: targets the 70 per cent who went offline or free, models 7,560 recovered — more than double Option A's count, and 1.8 times its rate per rupee. Cost: the largest bet, still net −₹0.80 crore in year one, and it draws focus from engineering.

Option C — Stay the course on feature parity

Continue the ₹2.8 crore already budgeted for matching rivals feature-for-feature, with no new pricing or hybrid-trust move. Upside: cheapest, no new organisational bet, stays credible in category comparisons. Cost: built on the diagnosis Exhibit 2 contradicted, and Exhibit 3 credits it with no recovered subscribers.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 tell you about who Gyanodaya's aspirants "hire" when they stop paying, versus the competitor the board is worried about?
  2. Why does Option A show a net loss in Exhibit 3 despite recovering real subscribers?
  3. Karan Mehta wants a story for Series C diligence; Vikram Oberoi wants to protect institutional pricing. Can one recommendation satisfy both?
  4. Given ₹8 crore and bandwidth for one initiative, not ₹10.5 crore for three, which option would you recommend on 16 October, and what would you have Karan tell the investors?

8. A note for the learner

The lens here is simple to state and easy to skip under pressure: your real competitor is whatever the customer hires today to get the job done, not the company that merely looks like you on a slide. Gyanodaya's board, primed by a visible price cut, reached for the obvious frame — Gurukul is a rival app, so the fight is on price and features. Exhibit 2 shows that frame captured only 16 per cent of the churn; the rest was never competing on category terms at all. A coaching institute and a WhatsApp group have no "pricing plan," yet they won the job anyway, because trust and local reputation are also ways of getting an aspirant through an exam.

A well-reasoned answer establishes where customers actually went before proposing a response, prices every option against that evidence rather than how defensible it sounds in a boardroom, and treats bandwidth as a real constraint — the choice is which single bet the team can actually deliver in two quarters.

On that basis, Option B is the defensible path, even though it is Exhibit 3's most expensive line and does not pay back in year one. It targets where four in five lapsed subscribers actually went, recovers them at nearly double Option A's rate per rupee, and builds trust a well-funded rival cannot match by cutting prices further. Option A should be named honestly as a narrow, money-losing move answering investor anxiety rather than churn; it may merit a small allocation for the genuinely price-sensitive 16 per cent, not as the main response. Option C is the quiet trap: cheap and defensible in the language of category competition, while Exhibit 2 already shows that language measures the wrong market.
